doc.title: Mona Hinton interviewed by Milt Fillius and Michael Woods, Scottsdale, Arizona, March 4, 1995

title: Breaking into New York studio work and the Rhythm Section
summary: After Calloway, Milt was hired by Jackie Gleason for a record date, then got steady studio calls and formed the New York Rhythm Section.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Studio work and jingles: New York session life

blocks.x: Oh, I think he got that always. In the Calloway band, and then — I’ll tell you what happened — he came to New York after he left Calloway’s band, and he was walking down the street one day and he ran into Jackie Gleason and his manager Bull. So Jackie, well Milton knew Jackie when he was, when only the musicians were laughing at his jokes, when they used to buy him a drink, so but he, as I said the day he ran into Milton he said to Milton said, “well what are you doing.” And Milton says, “well I’m looking for a job.” I mean Milt was just freelancing a little bit around because he’d just come off the road. And so Jackie says to Bull he says, “you know we have a record date tomorrow with Bobby Hackett,” so he says, you know, “let’s get Milt.” So Bull says, “you already have a bass player.” He said, “Well now we’ve got two.” And he hired Milton to do that record date. Well consequently there were no black musicians were recording in those days like that. And but when he went in, the A&R man and the conductor and everyone saw that Milton was qualified, and this was, a contractor came over and got his name and the address and said well how can I contact you if I need you, and that’s how he became involved, because he was qualified. You see it didn’t make any difference whenever a contractor would call, it could be, he never asked who it was for. He would call and say, “is Mr. Hinton free at ten o’clock on Tuesday” or whatever it is, and I had an appointment book, and, “yes he’s free.” “Well have him at RCA Victor or Capitol or Columbia Studio at such and such a time. Now when he left home he didn’t know whether it was a rock ‘n roll, whether it was with Stravinsky, whether it was with Barbra Streisand, he didn’t, or with a — he didn’t know who it was for. Guy Lombardo, you know, it could be anybody. And these were the people that he just went there, they put the music up there, and he had to be on time, he says that, not looking for a place to park or not adjusting your strings, when that conductor’s baton came down across his nose you were there to get that first note. And so Milton believes in punctuality. But these are the

things that got him started. And once they knew that he was qualified, he could read anything, play anything, and so he just started getting more work than he could handle. And then there for a long time, Osie Johnson the drummer, Barry Galbraith, the guitar player, Hank Jones the piano player, and Milton, they would work, they would do at least three sessions a day — 10-1, 2-5 and 7-8 every day. They were called the New York, the New York Rhythm Section. And they did that for years. As I say that’s because they were all qualified. They didn’t have to ask can you play this or that. It’s an interesting thing, what’s his name? Lee? Bill Lee’s son? Milton just did a date with him last year. He always wanted to do a date with Milton and Milton says, I can’t tell you the name of it, but you see Milton made his first recording date in 1930. And he has worked with every group of musicians, every generation, from that day up to the present day. He, well as a matter of fact, last, two weeks ago he did the soundtrack for what is it, “Clockers” that was, what’s his name, Lee? What’s his name? Bill Lee’s son, the movie guy?
